reason: Start with Hobbes’s account of authorization to understand the basis of obedience before testing its limit.
expectation: I expect an account of how people authorize a sovereign, though I’m unsure how it connects to protection.

alternatives.reason: Locke’s consent and majority rule also address a goal, but I’ll follow Hobbes first.

effect: Hobbes links authorized sovereign power to peace, making the loss of protection the next test.
reaction: The qualification that concentrated power may fail is useful.
reason: Test the stated limit of obedience when the sovereign can no longer protect a subject.
expectation: I expect protection’s failure to affect the subject’s obligation to obey, though the precise limit is unclear.

alternatives.reason: Locke’s account is also relevant, but I want to finish the Hobbes comparison first.

effect: Hobbes’s limit turns on lost protection, not merely disagreement; the Locke goal remains.
reaction: That distinction makes the limit clearer.
reason: This is the only offered combination, and it begins Locke’s account of political consent.
expectation: I expect an explanation of how consent relates to majority decisions, before testing arbitrary rule.

effect: Locke treats majority-authorized government as a trust to protect lives, liberty and possessions, setting up the test of arbitrary seizure.
reaction: The distinction between consent and unlimited authority is clear.
reason: The only offered combination tests how Locke judges rulers who breach that trust.
expectation: I expect arbitrary seizure to constitute a breach of trust and potentially justify resistance.

effect: Locke’s breach-of-trust argument provides a distinct basis for resistance from Hobbes’s protection-based limit; both goals are complete.
reaction: The concrete harvest seizure makes the contrast clearer, and the qualification about resistance succeeding is useful.

mostWorthwhile.text: Testing arbitrary seizure against Locke’s account was most worthwhile: the harvest example gave the abstract idea of breached trust a concrete consequence.

leastWorthwhile.text: The initial statement that sovereign power can secure peace felt less engaging than testing its limits; it was mostly setup.

surprise.text: Hobbes’s account allows the duty to obey to end when protection is lost, rather than treating obedience as unconditional.

arbitrary.text: No action felt purposeless, though the last two combinations were the only gameplay options offered, so they involved little choice.

continue.text: I would continue: comparing concrete limits on obedience made the competing theories clearer, though I’d hope for more meaningful choices.
